title: Colby’s Empty Charm Offensive
gist: Elbridge Colby's Southeast Asia tour message of deeper U.S. engagement was undercut in real time by concurrent U.S. actions — a carrier gap in the Pacific, cutbacks to South Korea drills, and a new transshipment-tariff crackdown naming Southeast Asian economies — while Indonesia's navy embarrassingly joined a China drill near Taiwan, illustrating both waning U.S. credibility and Indonesia's growing strategic drift under Prabowo.

themes.theme: Colby's message undercut by concurrent U.S. actions

insights.claim: Colby told Southeast Asian audiences the U.S. would be less ideological than previous administrations and notably omitted any mention of China or the South China Sea in his Manila speech, despite that being his host's biggest security concern.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: A deliberate omission of China from a Manila security speech signals a softer, less confrontational messaging strategy toward the region that regional capitals wary of U.S.-China tension might welcome — worth tracking for consistency in future U.S. statements.
insights.quote: which were hidebound by outdated convention or rigid adherence to liberal dogma
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Colby, who also visited Indonesia'

insights.claim: The same week as Colby's tour, the U.S. announced it would have no aircraft carriers in the Pacific for a couple of months as the USS George Washington left to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln in the Gulf, and Trump ordered military exercises with South Korea cut back, citing Seoul's non-help against Iran and his 'very good relationship' with Kim Jong Un — undermining Colby's reassurance message.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Confirms and cross-references the carrier-gap and Korea-drill-cut signals reported elsewhere as directly damaging U.S. credibility with Southeast Asian allies during a live diplomatic tour — a concrete example of policy incoherence undermining stated strategy.

insights.claim: Analyst Aaron Connelly of The Economist noted the real problem is not carrier capacity in the region but 'the perception that the president wants summits with Kim Jong Un and Xi Jinping more than he wants to deter an attack by either one on American allies.'
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: A sharp framework distinguishing perception-of-priorities risk from raw military-capacity risk — useful lens for interpreting how allies discount U.S. deterrence commitments regardless of underlying force levels.
insights.quote: the perception that the president wants summits with Kim Jong Un and Xi Jinping more than he wants to deter an attack by either one on American allies

insights.claim: Colby praised both the Philippines and (in May, via Defense Secretary Hegseth) South Korea as 'model allies,' raising the question of what that label means when South Korea is simultaneously having its joint exercises cut back.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Inconsistent application of the 'model ally' label undermines its signaling value to other regional partners assessing what U.S. commitment actually guarantees.

themes.theme: Philippines: real deliverables but limits on U.S. asks

insights.claim: Colby and Philippine President Marcos announced new U.S.-Philippine Coast Guard patrols in the South China Sea, but Colby did not address Marcos's complaints about how the Iran war has created an energy crunch for the Philippines, and Marcos again raised the possibility of joint energy exploration with China in the South China Sea.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: The Philippines is actively hedging toward joint energy cooperation with China amid U.S.-linked energy-cost pain — signals Manila's alignment with Washington is conditional on the U.S. addressing tangible economic costs, not just security cooperation.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Colby's tour was not fruitless'

insights.claim: Marcos clarified that if there were a war in Taiwan, he would not allow the United States to conduct strikes from Philippine soil — a deliberate distancing from his prior remarks that the Philippines would 'inevitably' be dragged into a Taiwan war.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: A concrete walk-back of prior Taiwan-contingency commitments by a key U.S. treaty ally is a material data point for any U.S. Taiwan-conflict planning assumption that presumes Philippine base access.

themes.theme: The Great Transshipment Scam report targets Southeast Asia

insights.claim: A new U.S. government report, 'The Great Transshipment Scam,' estimated approximately $60 billion in illegally transshipped Chinese goods and flagged more than 40 countries with 'elevated illegal transshipment risk,' nine of them in Southeast Asia; Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam were classified as combining significant transshipment volumes with deeper China-linked supply-chain integration.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: A concrete $60 billion transshipment estimate and formal country flagging is a leading indicator of coming U.S. tariff-enforcement action against Southeast Asian re-export hubs — relevant for supply-chain and trade-flow risk in these four economies specifically.

insights.claim: Some companies that relocated from China to Southeast Asia to avoid Trump's first trade war are now reportedly looking at going back, as marginally higher Chinese tariffs are offset by China's enormous manufacturing efficiency, since the tariff gap between China and other countries is now smaller than before Trump's 2025 tariff salvo.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: A contrarian reversal-of-reshoring signal: the 'China plus one' manufacturing relocation trend may be partially unwinding as tariff-gap incentives shrink — relevant for Southeast Asian manufacturing FDI and China supply-chain exposure forecasts.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Even if China has the highest tariffs'

insights.claim: An Indonesian navy frigate briefly joined a naval exercise with a Chinese frigate in waters off Taiwan's east coast while returning from a joint exercise with Russia in Vladivostok, sparking a diplomatic protest from Taiwan and a U.S. statement urging a halt to China's 'continuous military pressure against Taiwan'; Indonesia's own statement downplayed the drill's location, suggesting it may not have fully grasped the sensitivity of its actions.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: An apparently unintentional Indonesian entanglement in Taiwan-strait geopolitics is a concrete sign of foreign-policy incoherence in Southeast Asia's largest economy, a factor relevant to Indonesia country-risk and its reliability as either a U.S. or China partner.

insights.claim: Analysts see the incident as a sign of Indonesia's growing strategic drift as President Prabowo Subianto places his personal, often unpredictable, imprimatur on foreign affairs — reminiscent of an earlier incident when a joint China-Indonesia statement mentioning 'overlapping maritime claims' directly contradicted Indonesia's long-held refusal to accept China's South China Sea claims and had to be disavowed.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: A pattern of unforced foreign-policy errors under Prabowo's personalized leadership style is a repeat-offense risk factor for Indonesia's nonaligned foreign-policy credibility and diplomatic predictability.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'This incident is reminiscent of Prabowo's visit to China'

insights.claim: Indonesian President Prabowo's approval rating fell to 51.1 percent in a July poll, down sharply from 81.2 percent in November 2025, amid growing dissatisfaction; he responded with promises of lower deficits and scaled-back state-control-of-raw-materials proposals that were welcomed by investors, with stocks climbing and bond yields falling, even as he continued talking up 6 percent growth targets for next year that rely heavily on state spending while private investment lags.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: A 30-point approval collapse in eight months plus a market-positive technocratic pivot (lower deficits, scaled-back raw-material export controls) is a directly tradeable signal already reflected in Indonesian stocks and bond yields — worth tracking whether the pivot is sustained given still-ambitious 6% growth targets reliant on state spending.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Dissatisfaction with Subianto is growing'
